query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Using closed-loop, high-throughput optimization based on automated solvothermal synthesis, accelerated aging, activity screening, machine learning, and Bayesian optimization will identify a modified multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst with improved combined low-temperature activity, poisoning resistance, and lifetime durability without increasing platinum-group-metal content.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst.
generation.intervention: Implement a closed‐loop high‐throughput optimization approach using automated synthesis, accelerated aging tests, activity screening, and machine learning (with Bayesian optimization) to iteratively tune the catalyst composition.
generation.conditions: The catalyst will be evaluated under simulated transient and low-temperature exhaust conditions (including temperatures below 150 °C) that contain relevant poisons such as H2O and NO, combined with accelerated aging protocols mimicking full vehicle lifetimes.
generation.structural_mediator: Optimized elemental distributions and microstructural features (e.g. more uniform solid solution, controlled nano-scale phase segregation) that enhance active sites for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation and mitigate poisoning and sintering.
generation.mechanism: The optimization algorithm identifies subtle compositional adjustments that fine-tune the local electronic and structural environment of the catalyst. This improves the binding energies at the active sites, promoting lower light-off temperatures and enhancing resistance to deactivation by poisons and long-term structural degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified near-equiatomic catalyst, the optimized catalyst is expected to show lower light-off temperatures (improved low-temperature activity), enhanced resistance to H2O and NO poisoning, and superior durability over accelerated aging cycles without increasing platinum-group-metal loading.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of the unmodified near-equiatomic multi-principal-element catalyst under identical exhaust and aging conditions.
generation.boundary: These improvements are expected to hold under laboratory-simulated exhaust conditions (including low-temperature transients and accelerated aging protocols) that accurately mimic real-driving emissions. The effectiveness may be limited if the simulation does not capture all real-world degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise compositional modifications and their magnitude of improvement are uncertain until the closed-loop optimization cycle is completed. Additionally, scaling the optimized catalyst synthesis from high-throughput screening to practical, large-scale production may reveal further challenges.

falsification_experiment.design: Set up a closed-loop high-throughput catalyst discovery platform that cycles through automated synthesis, accelerated aging, and activity screening. Compare the performance of catalysts identified by the optimization algorithm against the unmodified near-equiatomic baseline under standardized low-temperature exhaust and aging protocols.
measurements: Light-off temperature for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation
Catalytic conversion efficiency in the presence of H2O and NO poisons
Performance degradation metrics after accelerated aging (simulated lifetime)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If none of the catalysts discovered via the optimization protocol demonstrates a statistically significant reduction in light-off temperatures and improvement in poisoning resistance and durability compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
